title: Orders and Execution
tagline: Market, limit, stop, trailing, bracket and OCO orders, and the fill a backtest has to assume
summary: Weight research ends at a target. Order research starts at a message to a market: market, limit, stop, stop-limit, trailing stop, bracket and one-cancels-the-other. This course defines each message, the fill assumption a simulator must make, and the extra conventions of lots, futures contracts and intraday bars. Slippage and the spread are part of the definition of a fill.
overview: An order is not a weight. A target weight can be reached by a market order, by a passive limit, or not at all if the limit is never touched. The open library’s order examples exist to make that difference concrete: the same economic story — trend, or an RSI dip — is sent to the market as a market order, a limit, a stop, a bracket or a pair of competing orders. The reported summaries differ, and the course treats those differences as objects of study.

Each order type is a contract with a precise trigger. A stop becomes a market order when a price is touched. A stop-limit becomes a limit, which may not fill. A trailing stop moves with a favourable price and freezes when the price reverses. A bracket places a profit-taking limit and a protective stop together. One-cancels-the-other keeps two entry ideas and kills the loser. None of these is a prediction. Each is a function from a future path to a fill, a cancel, or a miss.

Futures and FX add a quantity convention: whole contracts, lot sizes, and a point value. Intraday bars add a session and a horizon so short that a few weeks of data, which is what several library examples report, cannot support a performance ratio. The course says so next to the definitions.

The last chapter is the gap between a printed price and a fill. A backtest that fills a market order at the next close, or a limit at its limit price whenever the bar’s range touches it, has chosen an assumption. Adverse selection — the tendency of passive fills to happen when the price is about to move through the order — is why a 100 percent win rate on a passive dip rule is not the good news it appears to be.
outcomes: Define market and limit orders and the information a simulator needs in order to declare a fill.
Define stop, stop-limit and trailing-stop orders, including when a stop-limit can fail to fill.
Define a bracket and a one-cancels-the-other pair, and trace both on a short price path.
Size an order in shares, FX lots and futures contracts given a point value and a volatility budget.
State a slippage model and a spread cost, and explain adverse selection against passive limits.
Explain why a reported win rate of 100 percent on a limit-entry rule is a statement about fills, not about expected growth.

history.title: The bid–ask spread as adverse selection
history.detail: Glosten and Milgrom modelled the spread as compensation for trading against someone who may be better informed. A passive fill is not a free improvement on a market order.

history.title: Continuous auctions and market impact
history.detail: Kyle’s model gave a linear relation between an informed order and the price move it causes, the ancestor of later impact formulas.

history.title: Optimal execution
history.detail: Almgren and Chriss posed execution as a trade-off between market impact and the risk of waiting, and derived schedules between a pure risk-minimising path and an aggressive one.

history.title: An electronic equity book
history.detail: Island ECN, launched in 1996, was one of the electronic limit-order markets that moved US equity trading off the floor and made the public book the object a simulator has to imitate.

history.title: Statistics of the order book
history.detail: Bouchaud, Mézard and Potters measured the order books of liquid Paris stocks and showed regularities — the distribution of incoming limit prices, the shape of the average book — that a fill model either respects or ignores.
